extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy (readers of Plato's Republic); general educated readers studying regime types and moral psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive criteria for evaluating forms of government (best to worst) and the corresponding character-types of citizens, based on Plato's account (Books VIII–IX) — listing features, causes of degeneration, and moral/educational requirements for a just city and just men.

rubrics_metrics.name: State promotes happiness of the whole city, not particular factions
rubrics_metrics.description: The best constitution is where the whole city might be in the happiest condition, and not any one tribe remarkably happy beyond the rest; the state promotes the happiness of the whole city, not their own particular interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrounding exposition emphasizes unity of purpose and avoidance of factional advantage; contrasted repeatedly with mixed or factional constitutions that privilege segments of the population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws govern and justice is established (guardians preserve constitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the laws govern and justice is established: the guardians of the laws are such in reality and preserve the constitution instead of destroying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text stresses that guardians must actually follow and protect the constitution (not simply hold office). If guardians deviate, the constitution degenerates.

rubrics_metrics.name: State is one, not many (political unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state must be one, not many — i.e., not split into hostile parties (no parties of poor and rich at war with each other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is tied to social harmony; a divided city (rich vs poor) cannot properly function or be happy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meritocratic mobility between classes
rubrics_metrics.description: If any descendant of the guardians be vicious, he is demoted to the other classes; if any descendant of the others be worthy, he is raised to the rank of the guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that birth alone should not fix class; promotion/demotion should follow merit and virtue, as part of maintaining justice and good governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education from infancy agreeable to the laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Children, receiving from their infancy an education agreeable to the laws of the constitution, grow up to be worthy men and observant of the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education is presented as the 'grand point' to be attended to; early and constitution-aligned instruction is crucial to produce virtuous citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-and-education system must cultivate four cardinal virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The system, both of laws and education, should be contrived to produce the virtues of fortitude, temperance, wisdom, and justice in the whole city and in individual citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four virtues are the metric by which the city and its citizens are judged; institutions should be designed toward them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of principle of single virtue vs many vices
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there is but one principle of virtue, the forms of vice are manifold; political regimes correspond to different species of soul and vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the conceptual framework: evaluate regimes by the dominant vice they instantiate and the single virtue they lack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambitious (Cretan/Spartan) republic — institutional features
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambitious (Cretan/Spartan) republic: honors rulers, has military emphasis (common meals, gymnastic exercises, contests of war), spurns agriculture and mechanical arts among guardians; selection mistakes can arise from misapplied musical/number rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato describes how mixed geniuses and improper selection among guardians produce a republic that imitates aristocracy in some ways and oligarchy in others; prevalence of contentious and ambitious spirit is diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambitious (Spartan) man — character traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Corresponding man is arrogant and rough toward inferiors, mild toward equals, extremely submissive to governors; fond of dignity and magistracy, values military performance over rhetoric or reason; becomes covetous with age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The life-history sketch (family influence, social rewards) explains how upbringing in such a republic produces the described character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy — institutional criterion: rule by wealth and legal valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchy is founded on men's valuations: the rich bear rule, the poor have no share; laws mark out the boundary of the constitution and regulate oligarchic power according to wealth (more to the more wealthy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oligarchy creates two cities in one (rich and poor), fosters rivalry, incapacity for sustained public military commitment, and leads to greater dishonor of virtue as wealth is honored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchic city social pathology (crime, drones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where almost all are poor except the governors, there will be concealed thieves, persecutors, sacrilegious persons, and workers of other evils; the magistracy restrains these as drones in a city with dangerous stings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes social consequences of extreme inequality: crime, social control, and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchic man — psychological/moral changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The ambitious man who loses fortune turns into an oligarchic man: humbled by poverty, he becomes parsimonious and avaricious, scraping together substance, making riches his highest honor and object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato gives a biographical account of how personal misfortune converts honor-seeking ambition into greed and narrow valuation of wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy — institutional features and freedoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy arises when the poor prevail; it is full of freedom of action and speech, liberty to do as one inclines, offices often distributed by lot, indulgence, neglect of education and discipline, and a variegated mix of manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democracy is praised for variety but criticized for excessive indulgence and equality without distinction; it contains all kinds of republics as models but tends toward disorder if education is neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic social dynamics: parties and redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The poor, prevailing over the rich, kill or banish some and share places in the republic; leaders rob the wealthy and give to the people to secure popularity; magistracies are often disposed by lot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains mechanisms (violence, redistribution) through which oligarchy can collapse into democracy and how leaders manipulate gains to maintain power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic man — character formation and vices
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic man grows up from parsimonious upbringing but, associating with drones and indulgent classes, becomes licentious, free from order, sees moderation as stupidity, temperance as unmanliness, and embraces luxury, impudence, and anarchy as liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage details symbolic redefinitions (vice labeled as virtue) and the internal 'faction' struggle in the soul paralleling political factions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive liberty breeds the conditions for tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: An excessive and unseasonable liberty in democracy leads to indulgence and then to extreme slavery; excessive liberty tends to change into excessive slavery — tyranny springs out of democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a causal criterion: look for unchecked liberty, indulgence, and the breakdown of law as predictors of slide toward tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rise of the tyrant — political mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: A tyrant arises when a popular leader, receiving an extremely submissive multitude, unjustly accuses citizens (including kin), abolishes debts, proposes land division, secures personal guards and the people's acquiescence, then uses force and purges to seize autocratic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text outlines political strategy used by would-be tyrants: exploiting popular fears, legal subversion, creation of personal armed followers, and violent elimination of opponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny — institutional and economic consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyrants maintain their guards by spending sacred things, levying light or heavy taxes, confiscating property; they raise wars to keep people poor and dependent; worthy men are eliminated, leaving the worst as guards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how tyranny impoverishes both city and tyrant, destroys civic goods, and necessitates predatory revenue-extraction and repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyrannical man — psychological profile and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The tyrannical man is governed by lawless desires (formerly only in sleep): savage, irregular, insolent, indulging in revelry, drunkenness, lusts, theft, pillage, deceit and violence; awake he acts on the same mad impulses, becoming the most wretched of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato contrasts the tyrant's inner life with his outward success; his life is actually miserable, fearful, and degraded despite apparent power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative happiness metric: kingship vs tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Kingly (regal) government is the best and produces most happiness; tyranny is the worst and produces greatest wretchedness — both for city and ruler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an evaluative standard: regimes should be judged by aggregate happiness and quality of life they produce for citizens and rulers alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and civic fragility: private wealth can mimic tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Private men who are rich and possess many slaves resemble tyrants in ruling over many; their security depends on the city's support; without it they become fearful about their households.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an analytic criterion: concentration of private wealth creates quasi-tyrannical dynamics and dependence on civic structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and law as watchmen/guardians of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: True learning and pursuits, and sound reasoning, are the best watchmen and guardians in the understandings of men beloved of the gods; where they are evacuated, false and boastful reasonings occupy the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforces the preventive role of education and law: their absence allows false opinions and vicious appetites to seize the soul and polity.
